1086.title: Shakti as a philosophy
1086.hook: a dancer finishes her performance, sees she has been fully seen, and leaves the stage
1086.howItsDone: The Samkhya Karika is studied in courses on Indian philosophy and in yoga schools, where its two principles, purusha and prakriti, are used to explain the Yoga Sutras.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's list: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of I, all one nature, and a higher one holding the world up.
screen: `ALL OF THIS IS MINE, AND THERE IS MORE.`

segments.voice: A dancer steps onto a stage. She moves, turns, tells a whole story with her hands and eyes. The audience watches. At some point the dance is complete: everything she came to show has been shown. So she stops, and walks off. That small scene is a picture from Samkhya, one of the philosophical schools of India, in a short book of verses called the Samkhya Karika. Samkhya isn't a hymn to a goddess. It's a cool, careful map of the world. But its picture of nature as a performer belongs right next to Shakti.
screen: `A DANCER, A STAGE, AN AUDIENCE.` → `EVERYTHING SHOWN, SHE STOPS.` → `WHO IS SHE DANCING FOR?`

segments.voice: Samkhya names two principles. Purusha: pure awareness, the one who watches. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes, body and mind included. The verse, in paraphrase: as a dancer stops dancing after showing herself to the audience, so prakriti stops after showing herself to purusha. First, who moves. Awareness, in this picture, doesn't dance; it just sees. All the motion belongs to nature. That's close to what this week has heard: Shiva still, Shakti moving. Second, why she dances. The Samkhya Karika says nature works for the sake of awareness, so that it can be seen, and so the watcher can be free. Another verse gives a homelier picture: the two together are like a lame man and a blind man. One can see but can't walk; the other can walk but can't see. Together they get somewhere. Third, the most tender line. Nothing, the text says, is more modest than prakriti: once she knows she has been seen, she does not show herself again. Fourth, the difference. In Samkhya, prakriti isn't a goddess and isn't worshipped. It's a principle in a system. Some goddess traditions take the picture and change its weight. In their reading the dancer is no lower than the watcher; she is the divine power itself, and some go further and say she is the watcher too. Both readings are part of Hindu thought. What the dancer gives everyone is a way to see motion: not as noise, but as a performance meant to be seen.
screen: `PURUSHA WATCHES. PRAKRITI MOVES.` · `SHE DANCES SO THE WATCHER CAN BE FREE.` · `NOTHING MORE MODEST THAN PRAKRITI.` · `A PRINCIPLE HERE, A GODDESS THERE.` · then, large: `SHOWN, SEEN, AND FREE.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let yourself be the audience: thoughts, sounds and feelings will come onstage, a plan, a passing car, an itch. Don't chase any of them off; watch each one the way you'd watch a dancer, with interest, until it has finished showing itself and leaves. If you pray, you can rest in the name you use for the divine; if you don't, rest in the watching.
Shakti as a philosophy. In Samkhya, prakriti dances for purusha, the watcher, and when she has been fully seen, she stops.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Nature dances so the watcher can go free. Until tomorrow.

1087.title: Shakti as a philosophy
1087.hook: all the gods gather before the goddess and ask her the plainest question there is: who are you?
1087.howItsDone: The Devi Upanishad, also called the Devi Atharvashirsha, is chanted by worshippers of the goddess, including during Navaratri, and is studied as a statement of the goddess as ultimate reality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samkhya's dancer: prakriti shows herself to the watcher, and once she's been fully seen, she stops.

Who are you? It's the question you ask a stranger at the door, a new neighbor, a voice on the phone. In a short text called the Devi Upanishad, it's the question every god asks the goddess. They come and stand before her, all of them together, and ask: who are you, great goddess? Yesterday, in Samkhya, nature danced and said nothing. Today she is asked to speak for herself. And her answer isn't a name, or a family, or a list of victories.
screen: `ALL THE GODS COME TO HER.` → `WHO ARE YOU, GREAT GODDESS?` → `TODAY SHE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's her answer, in paraphrase. I am of the very nature of Brahman. From me comes this world, made of prakriti and purusha, nature and spirit, the empty and the not-empty. I am joy and not-joy. I am knowing and not-knowing. First, she answers with Brahman. The ultimate reality Uma named for Indra in the Kena: here the goddess simply says, that's me. Second, the pair she claims. Samkhya kept prakriti and purusha as two: the dancer and the watcher, never the same. Here both come from her. She isn't only the dancer anymore; she is the dance and the one watching it. In this text, power isn't one half of reality. It's the whole, seen from the side that moves and gives. Third, the opposites. Empty and not-empty, joy and not-joy, knowing and not-knowing. She doesn't pick the comfortable half. In this text's picture, the gentle and the rough both sit inside her, not outside. Fourth, what the gods do next. The text has them bow and praise her: a question, an answer bigger than the question, and then worship. Not everyone on the Hindu path reads it this way; Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions name the highest reality Vishnu or Shiva. In this Upanishad, the goddess answers for herself.
screen: `I AM OF THE NATURE OF BRAHMAN.` · `PRAKRITI AND PURUSHA, BOTH FROM HER.` · `EMPTY AND NOT-EMPTY. JOY AND NOT-JOY.` · `THE GODS BOW, AND PRAISE HER.` · then, large: `WHO ARE YOU? I AM BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Notice one comfortable thing right now, warmth or a soft seat, and hold it for a few breaths. Then notice one uncomfortable thing, a tight shoulder or a worry, and hold that too, without pushing it away, letting both sit in the same space the way the goddess holds joy and not-joy. If you pray, you can rest in the name of the Devi, or the name you use for God; if you don't, rest in the space that holds both.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Devi Upanishad, the gods ask who she is, and she answers: of the nature of Brahman, the source of prakriti and purusha both.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Asked who she is, she answers with everything. I'll be here tomorrow.

1088.title: Shakti as a philosophy
1088.hook: a poet about to write a long poem asks for one thing first: that his words and their meanings stay together
1088.howItsDone: The opening verse of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is learned by students of Sanskrit and recited as an invocation, and images of Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half Parvati, stand in temples dedicated to Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Devi Upanishad: the gods asked who are you, and the goddess answered, of the nature of Brahman.

A poet sits down to write a long poem about the kings of Raghu's line, one king after another. And the first thing he writes isn't about any king. It's about a word and its meaning. The poet is Kalidasa, whose Parvati this path met in the forest not long ago. Before he tells a single story, he bows to a couple. Not a king and queen: Shiva and Parvati. And he chooses one picture to say how close they are.
screen: `A LONG POEM OF KINGS.` → `FIRST: A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` → `HE BOWS TO A COUPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Joined like word and meaning, for the sake of understanding word and meaning, I bow to the parents of the world, Parvati and Shiva. First, the picture. Word and meaning aren't two things that happen to be in the same room. A word without meaning is just noise. A meaning needs some sign to carry it. They are two, and they are never apart. That's how close the poet says the goddess and the god are. Second, why he asks. He bows to them for the sake of understanding word and meaning. He's about to spend a whole poem putting words to work, so he asks the couple who are word and meaning to help his words mean something. It's a writer's prayer, and a clever one: the same image twice, once about God and once about his craft. Third, the parents of the world. Kalidasa doesn't call Parvati a helper or a shadow. Mother and father together are where the world comes from. That fits this week: Shiva can't stir without Shakti; Uma names Brahman; nature and spirit both come from the goddess. Fourth, the image people know. In temples and paintings, Shiva and Parvati are sometimes shown as one body, half him and half her, divided down the middle: Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman. The poet's word and meaning and the sculptor's single body say the same thing in two arts. In both pictures, Shakti isn't a second god beside the first. She's the other half of the same one.
screen: `JOINED LIKE WORD AND MEANING.` · `A WRITER'S PRAYER, TWICE OVER.` · `THE PARENTS OF THE WORLD.` · `ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.` · then, large: `TWO, AND NEVER APART.`

segments.voice: Choose one simple word that matters to you, home, mother, peace, a name, and say it once, silently, then watch what arrives with it: a picture, a feeling, a face. Say it again, slowly, and rest wherever the sound and the sense meet. If you pray, you can choose the name of the goddess, or Shiva, or the name you use for God.

Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Two, like a word and its meaning, and never apart. See you tomorrow.

1089.title: Shakti as a philosophy
1089.hook: a hymn in the Rig Veda where a goddess speaks in the first person: I move with the gods, I bend the bow, I breathe out like the wind
1089.howItsDone: This hymn, Rig Veda 10.125, is known as the Devi Sukta or Vak Sukta; it is chanted in goddess worship, and some recite it alongside the Devi Mahatmya.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kalidasa's bow: Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning.

I. A hymn can be sung to Agni, to Indra, to the dawn. This one in the Rig Veda is sung by someone. The speaker is Vak, a goddess whose name means speech, and tradition names her as the seer of the hymn herself. The whole hymn comes from her own mouth. I move with the gods. I hold them up. I bend the bow. I breathe out like the wind. Today, the last day on Shakti as a philosophy, a Vedic hymn answers in the first person.
screen: `NOT SUNG TO HER. SUNG BY HER.` → `VAK: THE GODDESS WHO IS SPEECH.` → `SHE SPEAKS AS I.`

segments.voice: Here is some of the hymn, in paraphrase. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus, with the Adityas and all the gods. I hold up Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni. I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures. Through me eats the one who eats, the one who sees, breathes and hears. Without knowing it, they live in me. I bend the bow for Rudra. I breathe out like the wind, taking hold of all the worlds. Beyond the sky, beyond this earth: so great have I become. First, she holds the gods up, not the other way around. That's the Saundarya Lahari's Shiva who couldn't stir, in another key. Second, she's inside ordinary acts: eating, seeing, breathing, hearing. Whoever does those, the hymn says, does them through her, without knowing it. That's the Shvetashvatara's hidden power, hidden in plain breath. Third, she arms the god. She bends the bow for Rudra, the fierce one. Power here isn't only gentle. It defends. Fourth, the widest: she holds all the worlds, and says she has gone beyond the sky and the earth. Inside everything, and beyond it. Put that beside the Devi Upanishad's answer, I am Brahman, and you can hear why some in goddess traditions hold this hymn close. In their reading, power isn't something the divine has. It's what the divine is, when it speaks for itself. Tomorrow the path turns to another Vedic hymn to a goddess, this time sung to her: the Sri Sukta.

segments.voice: Let the breath come on its own, and notice it as the hymn does: something breathing through you, not only something you do. Then add hearing, the sounds arriving without effort, and seeing, light on the eyelids or the room, and rest in all of it at once. If you pray, you can hold the word Devi, or Ma, with the out-breath; if you don't, just rest in the breathing.

1090.title: the Sri Sukta
1090.hook: a hymn heard when lamps are lit for Lakshmi opens with a portrait made of gold, silver and moonlight
1090.howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted in Lakshmi worship, including in some homes and temples at Diwali, with lamps lit and offerings set before an image of the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last day on Shakti as a philosophy: Vak, the goddess who speaks for herself. I move with the gods; I breathe out like the wind.

Lamps along a windowsill. A doorway swept clean. A small plate of sweets, a few coins, a picture of a goddess seated on a lotus. In some homes and temples, when Lakshmi is worshipped, a hymn in old Vedic Sanskrit is chanted over all of it. It's called the Sri Sukta, the hymn to Sri. Yesterday the goddess spoke for herself. Today the voice turns around: a singer calls to her, and asks her to come. The path will walk this hymn slowly, one piece at a time.
screen: `LAMPS, A SWEPT DOOR, A LOTUS.` → `THE HYMN TO SRI.` → `NOT SUNG BY HER. SUNG TO HER.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sukta means a hymn. Sri is the goddess, the one also called Lakshmi, and the word sri is heard as radiance, beauty and good fortune all at once. The hymn sounds Vedic: a singer, a fire, a request. Second, the first picture. The opening verse calls her golden in color, wearing garlands of gold and silver, shining like the moon, made of gold. Not a story, not a battle, just light. Gold and silver are wealth, yes. But nobody can own moonlight, store it, or spend it. The hymn sets them side by side, and some readers hear the point there: the fortune the singer wants is bright the way gold is, and also cool and freely given, the way the moon is. Third, where this sits on the path. The last stretch was about Shakti as power: the power that lets Shiva stir, that holds up the gods, that breathes through every breath. In goddess worship, Lakshmi is that power seen as abundance. Not only money: food on the table, health, a peaceful house, a good name. Teachers read the hymn in more than one way. Some keep it plain, a household asking not to go without. Others hear it inwardly, as a prayer for the brightness of a good life. The hymn doesn't choose. Fourth, how it begins: with a request to someone else, the fire, to bring her. That's tomorrow. Today, just the portrait: golden, garlanded, moonlit.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that's like gold, something you worked for or keep safe, and hold it for a few breaths, with thanks. Then bring to mind one thing like moonlight, something good you never earned and can't own: a friend's laugh, a clear night, a stranger's kindness. If you pray, you can name them both before Lakshmi, or before God, in the words you already use.

1091.title: the Sri Sukta
1091.hook: the hymn wants the goddess of fortune in the house, and the first one it speaks to is the fire
1091.howItsDone: In Lakshmi worship and Vedic rites, the Sri Sukta is chanted before a lamp or sacred fire, and some households light small lamps at Diwali to welcome the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta opened with a portrait: golden, garlanded in gold and silver, shining like the moon.

There's an old way to meet someone important: don't knock on their door yourself. Ask someone who already knows them, a cousin, a teacher, a friend of a friend, to make the introduction and bring you by. The Sri Sukta does exactly that. The singer wants Sri, the goddess of fortune, in the house. But the first words of request aren't spoken to her at all. They're spoken to the fire. Today, the end of that opening verse. Bring her to me, fire.
screen: `ASK SOMEONE WHO KNOWS THEM.` → `THE FIRST REQUEST ISN'T TO HER.` → `BRING HER TO ME, FIRE.`

segments.voice: The verse ends, in paraphrase: O Jatavedas, bring Lakshmi to me. Jatavedas is a name of Agni, the fire. Start with what the fire does in the Vedas. In the opening hymn of the Rig Veda, Agni is praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who will bring the gods here. Offerings go into the fire, and the fire brings the gods. Fire is the go-between. So when the Sri Sukta asks the fire to bring Lakshmi, it's asking fire to do its old work. Second, the little word for bring: avaha, bring here, carry this way. It isn't go and get. It's closer to a host saying to a friend: please bring her by. The singer stays home, keeps the fire going, and trusts the fire to make the introduction. Third, what's quietly assumed. You can't ask a fire for anything if none is burning. A household fire needs fuel, care and someone to watch it, and the request depends on that steady small work. Some readers hear a plain lesson in it: fortune is asked for through something you already keep alive at home. Fourth, the lamp. In some Hindu homes, small lamps are lit when Lakshmi is welcomed, especially at Diwali, the festival this path met in its first year, along windowsills and doorsteps. The go-between is now small enough to sit in a clay cup. Great altar or one wick in oil, the shape of the request is the same: a light is kept burning, and the goddess is asked to come by it.

1092.title: the Sri Sukta
1092.hook: a paycheck that's gone by Thursday, and a hymn that asks fortune not just to come, but to stay
1092.howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted by some Hindus in Lakshmi worship at home and in temples, including at Diwali, and some families recite it on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta asked the fire, Jatavedas, to bring her: fire as the go-between. Today, one more word, and the end of a week.
screen: `THE SRI SUKTA.` · `BRING HER TO ME, FIRE.`

segments.voice: A paycheck lands on a Friday. By Thursday it's mostly spoken for: rent, groceries, a birthday present, the car making that noise again. It comes in through the front door and slips out the back. Old hymns knew this too. The Sri Sukta has already asked the fire to bring the goddess close. Now it asks again, and adds a request that sounds almost like a worry. Don't just come. Stay.
screen: `IN THROUGH THE FRONT DOOR.` → `OUT THROUGH THE BACK.` → `DON'T JUST COME. STAY.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase. Bring to me, Jatavedas, that Lakshmi who does not go away, in whom I may find gold, cattle, horses, and people. The fire is still the go-between. What's new is the word for her, one long Sanskrit word, anapagamini: the one who does not go away. Notice the honesty in it. You only ask for someone who stays if you know what it is when someone leaves. The hymn admits, near its start, that fortune can come and go. Tradition says it more bluntly elsewhere, calling Lakshmi restless. Here the singer simply asks. Not for a windfall, which arrives and leaves, but for a fortune with roots, a presence that settles into the house. Now the list. Gold, cattle, horses, people. In the hymn's world, wealth walks around. It eats. It needs a barn and water and someone up early to tend it. And the last thing on the list isn't a thing at all: people. Some readers hear family there; others hear a household full of helpers and guests. Either way, the hymn counts the faces around the table among the riches. So the line holds a small picture of what staying looks like. Not a pile in a vault. A household that keeps going: animals fed, people gathered, the fire tended. And the week behind it: Shakti as a philosophy, the goddess as the power moving through everything; then a portrait in gold, silver and moonlight; then the fire asked to make the introduction. Today the request gets specific. Come, and don't go.
screen: `THE FIRE IS STILL THE GO-BETWEEN.` · `THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.` · `GOLD, CATTLE, HORSES, PEOPLE.` · `A HOUSEHOLD THAT KEEPS GOING.` · then, large: `COME, AND DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Notice the breath first: it leaves, and it comes back, without being asked. Then bring to mind one good thing in your life that hasn't gone away, a friend who keeps answering, a kitchen, a song that's still there, and rest with it, letting the thanks be quiet. If you pray, you can name it before Lakshmi or before God, in the words you already use; if you don't, let the steady thing be enough.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn to Sri, called Lakshmi, which asks the fire to bring her, and asks for the one who does not go away.
